drip.author: FocalPointFran
drip.title: Fall wedding season means golden hour lands in the middle of cocktail hour and I have to steal the couple
drip.body:
In June, sunset comes after dinner and speeches and everyone's relaxed. By late September the light has gone gold before the salads are served. So part of my job this time of year is gently kidnapping two people from their own party for fifteen minutes.

What works: I tell couples at the consultation that golden hour is non-negotiable and we set a time for it. The planner is in on it, nobody makes an announcement, and we slip out a side door. Fifteen minutes, the best frames of the day, back before anyone finishes their drink. What doesn't work: 'right after the toasts.' The toasts always run long, and the sun does not care about the best man's third story.

comments.author: LensAndLatte
comments.body: the sun does not care about the best man's third story belongs on every camera strap. same problem in the city this month, golden hour suddenly starts before 7 and I'm still at my desk

comments.author: RAWfiles
comments.body: Fifteen minutes of good light beats two hours of bad. One thing I'd add: in the fall it goes fast once it goes. Blue hour right after is short, but it's a gift for the couple-in-front-of-the-glowing-venue shot.

replies.author: FocalPointFran
replies.body: Blue hour with the reception lights coming through the windows is my secret last frame. Weirdly, couples end up printing that one bigger than the gold.

comments.author: regina_mona
comments.body: Out here the kidnapping has to account for wind. Fifteen minutes of gold and a veil that's determined to make it to Manitoba.

comments.author: ISO_a_good_time
comments.body: Stealing the couple for fifteen minutes isn't kidnapping. It's just a short exposure.

drip.author: regina_mona
drip.title: Harvest dust is the best diffusion filter Saskatchewan has ever given me
drip.body:
It's harvest out here, which means every evening there's a combine somewhere throwing a long cloud of dust into the air. Get on the right side of it around sunset, with the light behind the dust, and the whole field glows like the sky is on a dimmer switch. No filter I own does it better.

A few things I've learned the gritty way. Shoot from the road or ask first, because farmers are busy and it's their land and their living. Keep a lens hood on and a blower in your pocket, since that glow gets into everything. And don't chase the combine. Pick a spot where it'll come back toward you on the next pass and wait. Combines are more patient than photographers and a lot more predictable.

comments.author: northof60
comments.body: Our version up here is ice fog in deep winter. Same trick, light behind it, and the whole world goes soft. Yours has a working field in it though, which is a better story.

comments.author: RAWfiles
comments.body: Backlit dust is one of those things where the camera sees more than your eye does. Expose for the brightest part of the glow and let the combine fall into silhouette. And the blower tip is real. Wiping a dusty front element with your shirt is how you end up with a scratch and a permanent regret.

replies.author: regina_mona
replies.body: Learned the shirt lesson years ago. That lens still has a tiny souvenir that shows up in every backlit shot I take with it.

comments.author: LensAndLatte
comments.body: city person, genuinely jealous. the closest toronto gets is a leaf blower on a sunny afternoon, and yes I have photographed that

comments.author: FocalPointFran
comments.body: Pick a spot and let it come back to you is the whole philosophy of photographing a wedding reception too. Never chase the flower girl. She's coming back around.

drip.author: northof60
drip.title: The dark nights are back in Yellowknife, and so is the aurora. My starting settings for anyone trying it this fall.
drip.body:
All summer the sky barely got dark enough to bother. Now it's properly dark by late evening and the lights have already been out a few times, which is no big deal (it's a huge deal, every single time).

For anyone who gets a clear night and some green this fall, here's where I start. Tripod, obviously. Widest lens you have, wide open, around f/2.8 if it'll go there. Manual focus on a bright star using live view, then tape the focus ring so you don't knock it. ISO 1600 to 3200. Exposures somewhere between 2 and 10 seconds, shorter when the aurora is moving fast so it doesn't smear into a green blob. Shoot RAW so you can fix white balance later. And keep a spare battery in an inside pocket, because the cold drains them faster than you'd think.

comments.author: RAWfiles
comments.body: Shoot RAW is the one piece of advice I never need talking into. The tape on the focus ring is the tip people skip and then lose a whole night of soft stars to. Ask me how I know.

replies.author: northof60
replies.body: Everyone learns the tape lesson exactly once. Mine was a forty-minute show, every frame beautifully out of focus.

comments.author: regina_mona
comments.body: We get aurora down in Grasslands some nights too, lower on the horizon and a bit shy about it. Same settings work, just with a coyote soundtrack.

comments.author: ISO_a_good_time
comments.body: Aurora moving too fast for the shutter is so relatable. Some nights I can't keep up either, but I try to stay positive. Or at least not negative.

comments.author: LensAndLatte
comments.body: adding this to the list of things my balcony light pollution will never allow. saving the settings for the day I finally drive far enough north

late_comments.author: ISO_a_good_time
late_comments.body: Found this thread while deciding whether to haul the big camera on a fall colour walk. Took the phone. Came home with my favourite shot in months. I may have to start phoning it in more often.
